# Gas gangrene

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Wound, soft tissue, bone, and joint infections > Gas gangrene*

[Original Article Link](/library/Uf0bl2)

---

## Summary

Gas <u>gangrene</u> or clostridial myonecrosis is a life-threatening <u>necrotizing soft tissue infection</u> most commonly caused by the rapid <u>proliferation</u> and spread of <u>Clostridium perfringens</u>. <u>Traumatic gas gangrene</u> occurs in wounds with compromised blood supply, while <u>spontaneous gas gangrene</u> occurs from hematogenous spread from lesions in the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>. Gas <u>gangrene</u> manifests with excruciating muscle <u>pain</u>, <u>edema</u> with subsequent <u>skin</u> discoloration (red-purple to black), and <u>signs of sepsis</u>. Gas production leads to <u>crepitus</u> and a feathering pattern of gas on imaging. Treatment involves immediate <u>surgical debridement</u> with removal of all <u>necrotic</u> tissue in combination with <u>antibiotic therapy</u>. Even with treatment, gas <u>gangrene</u> has a high <u>mortality rate</u>.

---

## Etiology

### Traumatic gas gangrene [[1]](/library/1x12vQ0)




* <u>Pathogen</u> [[1]](/library/1x12vQ0)

* <u>Clostridium perfringens</u> (> 80% of cases): a gram-positive, obligate anaerobic, <u>spore-forming</u> bacterium

* Less common: <u>C. septicum</u>, C. histolyticum, C. novyi, C. sordellii

* Source: wounds with compromised blood supply create an optimal anaerobic environment for <u>C. perfringens</u> [[1]](/library/1x12vQ0)

* <u>Septic</u> surgical wounds or procedures (e.g., bowel and <u>biliary tract</u> <u>surgery</u>)

* Deep, penetrating wounds (e.g., knife, gunshot)

* <u>Open fractures</u>

* <u>Childbirth</u>, abortion, and other gynecological procedures





### Spontaneous gas gangrene [[2]](/library/j8d_m70)




* <u>Pathogen</u>: most commonly caused by <u>C. septicum</u>

* Source: hematogenous spread from lesions in the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u> 

* Gastrointestinal <u>malignancy</u> (e.g., <u>colon carcinoma</u>)

* <u>Diverticulitis</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

Ubiquitous <u>C. perfringens</u> spores contaminate a wound OR <u>C. septicum</u> spreads hematogenously from lesions in the gastrointestinal tract → bacterial reproduction under anaerobic conditions → ↑ secretion of <u>exotoxins</u>, especially C. perfringens alpha-toxin (a phospholipase lecithinase) → degradation of phospholipids → tissue destruction (myonecrosis), inhibition of <u>leukocyte</u> function, and gas production → gas separation into healthy tissue → further <u>colonization</u> and more local tissue destruction → further exacerbation of anaerobic conditions by the development of <u>edema</u>

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Incubation period</u>: hours to days

* Local signs and symptoms

* Excruciating muscle <u>pain</u>; initially, <u>pain out of proportion to physical examination</u>

* Massive <u>edema</u> with <u>skin</u> discoloration that progresses from bronze to red-purple to black and overlying <u>bullae</u>

* Sweet and foul-smelling or nonodorous discharge produced by anaerobic metabolic products

* <u>Crepitus</u>; : Palpation reveals crackling of the <u>skin</u> due to gas production (<u>skin</u> <u>emphysema</u>).

* Spreading infection (see “<u>Classic signs of inflammation</u>”)

* Systemic signs and symptoms

* Can progress to systemic infection within a few hours

* Early signs

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* Late signs

* <u>Shock</u>

* <u>Multiorgan failure</u>

* <u>Hemolytic anemia</u>

* <u>ARDS</u>

* <u>Kidney</u> and <u>liver</u> failure





![Gas gangrene](media/h6ijedu9k7rfa5xwahjkna0o.jpg)

Gas gangrene




> [!WARNING]
> Gas <u>gangrene</u> is a <u>medical emergency</u> that can rapidly progress to <u>multiorgan failure</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Perfringens perforates: <u>C. perfringens</u> causes gas <u>gangrene</u> that leads to severe tissue damage.

---

## Pathology

Histopathological findings include: [[3]](/library/i8dJm70)




* Myonecrosis and destruction of surrounding degenerative tissue (muscle, fat, <u>subcutaneous tissue</u>)

* Pathogens without inflammatory infiltrate

---

## Diagnosis

> [!WARNING]
> Gas <u>gangrene</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>; do not delay treatment to perform diagnostic studies.




### Approach [[1]](/library/1x12vQ0)[[2]](/library/j8d_m70)[[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Perform a <u>septic workup</u>.

* Obtain imaging for diagnostic uncertainty and/or to assess extent of infection.

* Confirm the diagnosis with surgical exploration and microbiological studies.





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/1x12vQ0)[[2]](/library/j8d_m70)




* <u>Septic workup</u>: including <u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u>, <u>lactate</u>, and <u>blood cultures</u>  [[3]](/library/i8dJm70)

* Additional microbiological studies 

* <u>Gram staining</u>: large, gram-positive rods

* Wound or tissue culture: double zone of <u>hemolysis</u> on blood agar  [[5]](/library/O8dI570)










### Imaging [[2]](/library/j8d_m70)[[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Modalities: <u>ultrasound</u>, <u>x-ray</u>, CT, or <u>MRI</u> depending on availability and patient stability

* Findings: characteristic feathering pattern of the <u>soft tissue</u> caused by gas pockets between muscle fibers

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Necrotizing fasciitis</u>

* <u>Vibrio vulnificus</u> infection; : may occur after an <u>open wound</u> is exposed to seawater contaminated with <u>V. vulnificus</u>

* <u>Group A streptococcal infection</u>

* <u>Rhabdomyolysis</u>

* <u>Pyomyositis</u>

* <u>Phlegmasia cerulea dolens</u>

* <u>Acute compartment syndrome</u>

* <u>Acute limb ischemia</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### Initial management [[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[6]](/library/cwca3e0)




* Stabilize patients using the <u>ABCDE approach</u>.

* <u>Manage septic shock</u> with <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u>.

* Begin empiric <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u>.

* Consult <u>surgery</u> immediately for <u>debridement</u>.

* Perform <u>emergency preoperative assessment</u>.

* Transfer to the OR and/or admit to an <u>ICU</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Gas <u>gangrene</u> requires prompt surgical exploration and <u>debridement</u>.




### <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> [[6]](/library/cwca3e0)[[7]](/library/Om0Ifg)




* Empiric <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u>

* Initiate <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u> as soon as gas <u>gangrene</u> is suspected.

* See “Necrotizing <u>SSTI</u>” in “<u>Empiric antibiotics for SSTIs</u>” for suggested regimens.

* <u>Pathogen</u>-specific <u>antibiotic therapy</u>

* Initiate <u>pathogen</u>-specific <u>antibiotics</u> as soon as clostridial infection is confirmed.

* First-line: <u>Penicillin G</u> DOSAGE PLUS <u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE [[6]](/library/cwca3e0)[[7]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* Alternatives [[8]](/library/Bedza60)

* A <u>carbapenem</u> (e.g., <u>meropenem</u>, <u>ertapenem</u>) PLUS <u>clindamycin</u>

* <u>Clindamycin</u> monotherapy





### Surgical and <u>wound management</u> [[2]](/library/j8d_m70)[[6]](/library/cwca3e0)




* Surgical management

* Prompt surgical exploration and <u>debridement</u> of all <u>necrotic</u> and devitalized tissue

* Potential <u>amputation</u> if an extremity is affected

* <u>Wound management</u>

* Reevaluate the affected area frequently; repeated <u>debridement</u> is often required.

* <u>Hyperbaric oxygen therapy</u> (<u>HBOT</u>) may be considered as an adjunctive treatment, if available.  [[6]](/library/cwca3e0)[[7]](/library/Om0Ifg)[[9]](/library/F8dgo70)[[10]](/library/48d3570)

* Monitor for and treat complications (e.g., <u>compartment syndrome</u>).
